messages.text: I get SSI. Can I also get food stamps?

**Yes, you can probably get food assistance (SNAP) and SSI together.** Getting SSI doesn't block you. Many people get both. Whether you qualify, and how much you'd get, depends on your household and income.

**What I found**
- A Tennessee legal-aid guide says people who get SSI or Social Security can be eligible for SNAP. It also says households with someone who is 60 or older or has a disability may qualify even with more income. ([TN Justice guide](https://www.tnjustice.org/_files/ugd/07a490_1c7e18672b53434a92037fcb95b8c572.pdf))
- Tennessee's income limit is unsettled. The official limit has been 130% of the poverty level. Some reports say the state moved to 200% in 2026. I couldn't confirm which is in effect, so you may land in "possibly." Please apply either way. ([Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap-in-tennessee.pdf), [Hoodline report](https://hoodline.com/2026/06/snap-shakeup-could-put-more-food-on-memphis-tables/))
- USDA's 2026-27 maximum monthly benefit is reported as $306 for one person and $562 for two. Your real amount is usually lower and depends on your income and costs. ([USDA 2027 cost-of-living memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf))

I couldn't open the USDA or Tennessee Department of Human Services pages myself. Those figures come from search summaries, so please treat them as rough.

**Next steps**
- Apply at [one of the state's official sites](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html), or call 211 for free local help. I couldn't confirm the state's phone number, so 211 can give you the right one.
- Only the state agency decides. If your income looks too high, you can still apply.

**Two questions so I can give a better estimate**
1. Who lives with you and shares food? Please give ages, and tell me if anyone else has a disability.
2. How much is your SSI each month? Does anyone in the home have other income, such as a job or child support?
Just me, I live alone. No one else has a disability. SSI is $994 a month, and I don't have any other income.

Thanks. With only your SSI of $994 a month, you look **likely** to qualify for food assistance (SNAP).

**Why**
- Reported 2026-27 USDA limits show about $1,729 a month in income before taxes for one person under the 130% rule. Your $994 is well under that. It would also be under the 200% limit, if that one applies. ([USDA 2027 cost-of-living memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf))
- Because you have a disability, the rules also let SNAP subtract certain costs from your income. I'm using a reported standard deduction of $217 a month for a one-person household and a maximum benefit of $306. That gives a rough starting estimate of **about $70 a month**.
- Your rent and medical costs could raise that amount. Any rent or utilities you pay can be subtracted from your income. Medical bills can be subtracted too, once they pass $35 a month. For people with a disability, the rent deduction has no upper cap.

This is only an estimate. I couldn't open the USDA or Tennessee pages directly. The numbers come from search summaries, so the state's final amount may differ.

**Two questions to firm up the estimate**
1. How much do you pay each month for rent or a mortgage? Do you pay for heating or cooling separately, or other utilities?
2. Do you pay for medical bills out of pocket each month, such as prescriptions, copays, or doctor visits? If so, about how much?

If it helps, you can also tell me your savings. That's optional. SNAP may have a savings limit, and I'd check it for you.

Rent is $450 a month. I pay the electric bill, and that covers heat and AC since it's all electric. No water or other bills that I know of.

For medical stuff, I have TennCare, so I don't really pay much out of pocket. Maybe nothing most months.

Your estimate went up. I now think you're **likely** to qualify for food assistance (SNAP), probably for about **$120 to $180 a month**. This is a rough estimate, and the state decides the real amount.

**How I got that**
- **Starting point:** Your SSI is $994 a month. SNAP subtracts a standard deduction of about $217, which leaves about $777.
- **Housing costs:** Your $450 rent plus your electric bill counts as a housing cost. Because heat and AC are in your electric bill, you may get a set utility amount from the state. The amount is often more than the bill itself.
- **Disability rule:** For people with a disability, SNAP subtracts the part of housing costs that is more than half of your remaining income. There is no upper cap.
- **Benefit math:** Your SNAP amount is the maximum benefit ($306 for one person) minus 30% of your remaining income.

I couldn't find Tennessee's set utility amount for 2026-27. So I tried a range of electric costs. That's why I'm giving a range and not one number.

Your medical costs look like $0 to $35 a month, so they probably won't change the estimate. If you start paying more than $35 a month out of pocket, tell the caseworker. It could raise your benefit.

**Sources**
- [USDA 2027 cost-of-living memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf) for the maximum benefit and standard deduction. I couldn't open it directly, so these figures come from search summaries.
- [USDA utility allowance page](https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/eligibility/deduction/standard-utility-allowances) for how utility allowances work. I couldn't open this page either, and it didn't give Tennessee's amount.

**Next steps**
- **Apply:** Use the [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html). I couldn't open it, so check the application link there. You can also call 211 for free help finding the right phone number or applying.
- **Have ready:** Your SSI award letter, your lease or a rent receipt, and a recent electric bill.
- **Savings:** Tennessee may have a savings limit, though reports say it may have been dropped for some households. Do you have savings of more than a couple thousand dollars? If so, tell me roughly how much and I'll look into it.
- **Accuracy:** Report your income and costs exactly as they are. If a benefit is paid in error, you may have to pay it back.

Would you like help checking whether you could also get any other programs? You already have TennCare, so food assistance is the main one left for a single adult.
Just about $50 in savings. Nothing more than that.

$50 in savings won't get in your way. Savings limits for SNAP are in the low thousands of dollars. Reports also say Tennessee may have dropped the limit for some households. Either way, $50 is far below it. I couldn't open the state's rules to confirm the exact limit.

**Where this leaves you**
- You look **likely** to qualify for food assistance (SNAP).
- My rough estimate is **$120 to $180 a month**. The state decides the real amount, and it could be different.
- Reasons: your income is well under the reported limits, you live alone, and you have a disability. Your $450 rent and your electric bill also raise your benefit.

**What to do next**
1. **Apply** on the [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html). I couldn't open that page, so look for the application link there. You can also call **211** for free help applying or to get the right phone number.
2. **Gather** your SSI award letter, your lease or a rent receipt, and a recent electric bill.
3. **Report** your income and costs exactly as they are. That protects you. If a benefit is paid in error, you may have to pay it back.

Only the state agency decides if you get SNAP and how much. If the answer is lower than you expected, you can ask them to explain it.

Would you like help getting ready for the interview? Applicants often have a short phone call with a caseworker.

**Sources**
- [USDA 2027 cost-of-living memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)
- [Sycamore Institute SNAP brief](https://sycamoretn.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap-in-tennessee.pdf)
- [Hoodline report on Tennessee's SNAP changes](https://hoodline.com/2026/06/snap-shakeup-could-put-more-food-on-memphis-tables/)

Tennessee's SNAP rules changed in mid-2026, and the sources I found are not fully consistent on the details.

- **SNAP gross income limit:** A June 2026 report says the Tennessee Department of Human Services has adopted broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), raising the SNAP gross-income threshold from 130% to 200% of total household gross monthly income and removing asset limits for some households. A TN Justice guide updated May 28, 2026 describes the same change, with the net income limit staying at 100% of the poverty line. The January 2026 Sycamore Institute brief predates the change and described the 130% gross limit as current, noting that the state was still pursuing the BBCE change pending legislative approval.
- **Monthly income table:** TN Justice's June 2026 guide lists gross monthly limits of $2,608 for a household of 1, $3,525 for 2, $4,442 for 3, $5,358 for 4, and $6,275 for 5. I'd treat these as the current figures to verify, since the guide's own table may reflect the pre-change limits.
- **SSI recipients:** The same guide says Tennesseans can also be eligible if they receive Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF)/Families First or Social Security (SSI/SSDI). It also notes that households with someone over age 59 or receiving disability benefits may qualify even if they have more income. Households where everyone is 18 to 64 face additional work requirements.
- **SSI income limits (2026):** A BenefitsUSA guide, a commercial source, reports that SSI countable income must be below $994 a month as an individual or $1,491 as a couple, with asset limits of no more than $2,000 in countable assets ($3,000 for couples). This is an SSI rule, not a SNAP rule, and I didn't find a source confirming how SNAP treats SSI income in Tennessee.

The sources don't clearly establish whether SSI recipients are automatically SNAP-eligible under the new BBCE rules or still subject to the income tests. Checking the TDHS website or the official BBCE policy would resolve that.

The FY2027 SNAP adjustments take effect October 1, 2026 and run through September 30, 2027. The USDA memo is dated August 21, 2026, and it covers maximum allotments, income standards, and deductions.

- **Maximum allotments:** For the 48 contiguous states and D.C., a four-person household's maximum is $1,023. One person: $306; two: $562; three: $808; four: $1,023; five: $1,217; six: $1,463; seven: $1,616; eight: $1,841. Hawaii's four-person maximum falls to $1,655, and Alaska's range is $1,306 to $2,027 (). Guam's four-person maximum is $1,507 and the U.S. Virgin Islands' is $1,315 ().
- **Minimum benefit and shelter cap:** The minimum benefit for the 48 states and D.C. rises to $25 (). The shelter cap rises to $769 ().
- **Large households:** The maximum for households of 18 or more is capped at $3,887 in the 48 states and D.C. ().
- **Gross income limits:** A single person in the 48 states, D.C., Guam, or the U.S. Virgin Islands has a gross monthly limit of $1,729, and a family of four has $3,575 (). Elderly and disabled households that qualify as separate households use 165% of the poverty level instead ().
- **Deductions:** The standard deduction for households of one to three in the 48 states and D.C. rises to $217 per month ().

Sources agree on these figures. The USDA memo is the primary source. The one caveat is that the secondary sources were written to describe the USDA memo, so the USDA document (fns.usda.gov, FY27 COLA page) should be treated as authoritative for any exact figure needed for a decision.
